title: RAG Production Stack
note: One story in three tracks: plain RAG, GraphRAG, and Intelligent Educator v2. Each step: problem -> why this component -> what it fixes, with input and output. 'evidence.status' says what the sources show: evidenced = the component is in the cited source; partly = the component is in the source, the explanation or arrangement is ours; ours = our own addition, not in the sources. Algorithm and metric ids must exist in the sister catalogues; build.py drops any id that does not.

prod.label: RAG in production architecture (human's Excalidraw)
prod.shows: Data layer (private documents, chunking, embedding, vector database), RAG pipeline layer (query service, routing, retrieval, augmented service, generate, caching), application layer (UI, mobile, admin), monitoring stack (Jaeger, dashboard, metrics, tracing, logging), container orchestration.

pipe.label: RAG pipeline (human's Excalidraw)
pipe.shows: Documents -> chunking -> embedding -> vector database; user query is embedded too; search -> augment -> generate. Caches in green: query cache, embedding cache, vector search cache, LLM response cache. Monitoring in brown: chunking efficiency, embedding performance, retrieval quality, response time, throughput (queries/second), error rate.

general.label: RAG general (human's Excalidraw)
general.shows: Indexing (documents -> index -> DB), retrieval (question -> relevant documents), generation (context window -> LLM -> answer).

parts.label: RAG parts (human's Excalidraw)
parts.shows: Query translation (multi-query, RAG-Fusion, decomposition, step-back, HyDE); routing (logical, semantic); query construction (text-to-SQL, text-to-Cypher, self-query retriever); indexing (chunk optimisation, multi-representation, specialised embeddings, hierarchical / RAPTOR); retrieval (ranking: re-rank, RankGPT, RAG-Fusion; refinement: CRAG; active retrieval: CRAG); generation (active retrieval: Self-RAG, RRR).

hr.label: HR policy copilot example (human's Excalidraw)
hr.shows: A RAG policy copilot over private policy documents; a restriction/security check (if the question hits a restriction, tell the user to go to HR); voice, style and language of the answer; prompt engineering vs fine-tuning vs RAG.

llmgr.label: LLM vs RAG vs GraphRAG (human's Excalidraw)
llmgr.shows: Basic: query -> LLM -> response. RAG: retriever adds retrieved text. GraphRAG: retriever adds retrieved triplets.

formula.label: GraphRAG formula (human's Excalidraw)
formula.shows: Input query q -> G-Indexing -> G-Retrieval p_theta(G | q, 𝒢) -> G-Generation p_phi(a | q, G) -> output a.

ie2.label: Intelligent Educator v2 - Architecture Plan (2026-10-02, status: proposed)
ie2.shows: Decisions 1-8, build order 0-7, evaluation, compute, local services (MLflow, Airflow, Metabase, Neo4j), embeddings on the IUST GPU, Postgres for vectors and graph, LLM provider (AvalAI), graph data model, access control.

lewis2020.label: Lewis et al. 2020, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (NeurIPS 2020)
lewis2020.shows: Fig. 1: query encoder + document index (MIPS) as the retriever, a seq2seq generator; retriever and generator trained end to end.

gao2023.label: Gao et al. 2023, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
gao2023.shows: Naive, Advanced and Modular RAG; pre-retrieval (query rewriting, routing), retrieval, post-retrieval (rerank, compress); evaluation (context relevance, faithfulness, answer relevance; noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness).

rfs.label: LangChain, RAG From Scratch (Lance Martin), overview figure
rfs.shows: README figure rag_detail_v2 (read 2026-10-09): Question -> Query Translation (decomposition: multi-query, step-back, RAG-Fusion; pseudo-documents: HyDE) -> Routing (logical, semantic) -> Query Construction (text-to-SQL, text-to-Cypher, self-query retriever) -> Graph DB / Relational DB / Vectorstore -> Documents -> Retrieval (ranking: re-rank, RankGPT, RAG-Fusion; refinement: CRAG; active retrieval: CRAG) -> LLM -> Answer; Indexing (chunk optimisation, multi-representation, specialised embeddings, hierarchical / RAPTOR); Generation (active retrieval: Self-RAG, RRR). The human's RAG-Parts Excalidraw redraws this figure.

edge2024.label: Edge et al. 2024, From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization (Microsoft)
edge2024.shows: Fig. 1 'Graph RAG pipeline': Source Documents -> Text Chunks -> Entities & Relationships -> Knowledge Graph -> Graph Communities (Leiden, hierarchical; graspologic) -> Community Summaries -> Community Answers -> Global Answer. Global answer = map (partial answers with a 0-100 helpfulness score, 0 dropped) then reduce (sorted by score into the final context).

msdocs.label: Microsoft GraphRAG documentation (indexing dataflow, query engine)
msdocs.shows: Indexing dataflow, 6 phases: compose TextUnits (1,200 tokens default), document processing, graph extraction (entities, relationships, optional claims; descriptions summarised), graph augmentation (hierarchical Leiden), community summarization (community reports), text embedding (entity descriptions, text units, community reports). Outputs: Parquet tables; vector store LanceDB by default (config page). Query engines: local (entities, relationships, covariates, community reports, text units), global (map-reduce over community reports), DRIFT, basic (top-k text units).

drift.label: Microsoft Research blog, Introducing DRIFT Search
drift.shows: Primer: the query (HyDE-expanded) is compared with the top-K community reports, giving an initial answer and follow-up questions; follow-ups run through a local-search variant (2 iterations at the time); output is a ranked hierarchy of questions and answers.

lightrag.label: Guo et al. 2024, LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation (HKU)
lightrag.shows: Sec. 3.1 graph-based text indexing (chunks -> LLM extracts entities and relations -> LLM profiling into key-value pairs -> deduplication); incremental update by union of node and edge sets, 'avoids rebuilding the whole index'. Sec. 3.2 dual-level retrieval: low-level keywords -> entities, high-level keywords -> relations (vector match), plus one-hop neighbours. README: query modes naive, local, global, hybrid, mix (default mix); storage backends incl. PostgreSQL, Neo4j, Milvus, Qdrant, MongoDB, OpenSearch (defaults NetworkX + NanoVectorDB, 'not suitable for production').

hipporag.label: Gutierrez et al. 2024, HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs (NeurIPS 2024)
hipporag.shows: Fig. 2. Offline: OpenIE (LLM: named entities, then triples) builds a schemaless KG; a retrieval encoder adds synonymy edges (cosine > 0.8). Online: LLM extracts the query's named entities -> linked to the nearest KG nodes -> Personalized PageRank from those seeds -> passages ranked by node probabilities. NeurIPS 2024.

hipporag2.label: Gutierrez et al. 2025, From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2, ICML 2025)
hipporag2.shows: Fig. 2: same offline indexing plus passage nodes ('contains' edges), query-to-triple matching instead of NER, an LLM recognition-memory filter of the top triples, then Personalized PageRank seeded by phrase and passage nodes.

peng2024.label: Peng et al. 2024, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
peng2024.shows: Fig. 2: G-Indexing (open KGs or self-constructed graph data), G-Retrieval (query enhancement, retriever, knowledge enhancement: merging, pruning), G-Generation with pre-, mid- and post-generation enhancement. Sec. 6.3 retrieval granularity: nodes, triplets, paths, subgraphs, hybrid. Sec. 7.2 / Fig. 6 graph languages: adjacency / edge table, natural language, code-like forms, syntax tree, node sequence; graph embeddings separately (7.2.2). The human's Detailed-Introduction-GraphRAG.png redraws this overview.

neo4jgr.label: Neo4j GraphRAG for Python (neo4j-graphrag) user guide
neo4jgr.shows: SimpleKGPipeline: loader -> text splitter -> chunk embedder -> schema (given or extracted) -> LLMEntityRelationExtractor -> KG writer -> entity resolver (on by default). Retrievers: VectorRetriever, VectorCypherRetriever, HybridRetriever, HybridCypherRetriever, Text2CypherRetriever, ToolsRetriever.

anthropic_cr.label: Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval
anthropic_cr.shows: An LLM-written context (50-100 tokens) is prepended to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing; retrieve top 150, rerank to top 20. Top-20 retrieval failure rate 5.7% -> 3.7% (contextual embeddings, -35%) -> 2.9% (+ contextual BM25, -49%) -> 1.9% (+ reranking, -67%).

aws_bkb.label: AWS, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases: how it works
aws_bkb.shows: Pre-processing: data source -> parser -> chunking -> embedding model -> vector index (OpenSearch, Aurora, Neptune, Pinecone, Redis, MongoDB, S3 Vectors). Runtime: query embedded -> vector search -> chunks added to the prompt (Retrieve / RetrieveAndGenerate, optional reranking; GenerateQuery for SQL). GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics: preview 2024-12, generally available 2025-03-07 (GA date from AWS What's New, read through a search summary: unverified).

azure_rag.label: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Design and develop a RAG solution
azure_rag.shows: Request flow: app UI -> orchestrator -> Azure AI Search -> top N results + query into the prompt -> language model. Data pipeline: chunking -> enrich chunks (title, summary, keywords) -> embed -> persist in the search index. Retrieval: vector, full-text, hybrid, multiple searches; end-to-end evaluation.

gcp_rag.label: Google Cloud Architecture Center, Infrastructure for a RAG-capable generative AI application using Vertex AI
gcp_rag.shows: Subsystems: data ingestion, serving, quality evaluation (+ databases). AlloyDB for PostgreSQL with pgvector as the vector store; Cloud Run, Pub/Sub, BigQuery, Cloud Logging and Monitoring. Vertex AI is now named Agent Platform on the page.

llamaindex.label: LlamaIndex documentation: ingestion pipeline and property graph index
llamaindex.shows: IngestionPipeline: transformations, per-node cache, docstore for upserts. PropertyGraphIndex: kg extractors (SimpleLLMPath, Implicit, Dynamic, Schema), retrievers (LLMSynonym, VectorContext, TextToCypher, CypherTemplate), stores (in-memory, Neo4j, Nebula, TiDB, FalkorDB).

otel_genai.label: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI
otel_genai.date: accessed 2026-10-09 (moved from opentelemetry.io; stability status unverified)
otel_genai.shows: Span and metric names for LLM calls, embeddings, retrieval and agents, so traces from different libraries look the same.

ragas.label: Es et al. 2023, RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (+ Ragas toolkit, Apache-2.0)
ragas.shows: Reference-free metrics defined in the paper: faithfulness, answer relevance, context relevance. The toolkit adds test-set generation.

intro.problem: An LLM alone answers from what it saw in training. It does not know your private documents, it cannot cite a page, and it invents facts when it does not know.
intro.why: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives the model the right passages at question time. But one 'retrieve then generate' box is not enough in production: each part fails in its own way.
intro.fix: So a production stack grows one component at a time. Each step below starts with the problem that the previous steps leave, says why the next component is added, and what it fixes.

rag.label: Plain RAG
rag.lede: Passages from a vector and a keyword index, ranked, then given to the LLM. Based on the human's diagrams RAG-General, RAG-Pipeline, RAG-Parts and RAG-in-Production-Architecture.

steps.title: Index the documents (offline, before any question)
steps.problem: The LLM cannot read a whole library for each question. It has a limited context window, and long input is slow and expensive.
steps.body: Before users ask anything, we cut each document into chunks. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector. We store the vectors in a vector database and the words in a keyword index. Chunk size matters: too small loses context, too large hides the answer. Structure-aware splitting, summaries per section and hierarchical trees (RAPTOR) are ways to improve this step.
steps.fixes: Search later works on small, addressable units, and each unit keeps its source page for citation.
steps.out: Chunks with ids, vectors in a vector DB, a keyword (BM25) index

evidence.ours: The keyword index next to the vector DB is ours; the human's diagrams show only the vector DB.

steps.title: The user asks a question
steps.problem: A question comes in from a web, mobile or admin interface. Some questions must not be answered, and some users must not see some documents.
steps.body: A query service receives the question from the application layer. First it checks restrictions: if the question is outside what the system may answer, it tells the user where to go instead (in the HR example: 'ask HR'). It also notes who asks, so that later steps search only the documents this user may read.
steps.fixes: Unsafe or out-of-scope questions stop early, and the user's identity travels with the question.
steps.out: An allowed question with a user scope, or a polite refusal

evidence.ours: Carrying the user scope to retrieval is ours (it is in the Intelligent Educator plan, not in the generic diagrams).

steps.title: Query translation: rewrite the question for the retriever
steps.problem: Users write short, vague or compound questions. The words of the question often differ from the words of the document, so the retriever misses the right chunk.
steps.body: An LLM rewrites the question into a form that a retriever handles better. Multi-query and RAG-Fusion write several versions and search with each. Decomposition splits a compound question into sub-questions. Step-back asks a more general question first. HyDE writes a hypothetical answer and searches with its embedding.
steps.fixes: Recall goes up: the right chunk is found even when the user's words do not match the document's words.
steps.out: One or more search queries (rewrites, sub-questions, a hypothetical document)

evidence.ours: The order 'translate before route' follows the human's RAG-Parts diagram.

steps.title: Routing: send the question to the right store and prompt
steps.problem: One index does not fit every question. Some answers are in a table, some in a graph, some in text; some questions need a different prompt.
steps.body: Logical routing lets an LLM choose the data source from the question. Semantic routing embeds the question and picks the prompt whose embedding is closest. For structured stores, query construction turns the question into a query language: text-to-SQL for relational DBs, text-to-Cypher for graph DBs, or metadata filters for a vector store (self-query retriever).
steps.fixes: Each question goes to the store and the prompt that can answer it, instead of one search for everything.
steps.out: A target store (vector, relational, graph) and a prompt template, with filters

evidence.ours: Linking semantic routing to the vector-similarity explainer is ours.

steps.title: Retrieval: vector search and keyword search, then fuse
steps.problem: Vector search finds meaning but misses exact terms, codes and rare names. Keyword search finds exact terms but misses paraphrases.
steps.body: We run both. Vector search compares the query vector with chunk vectors (cosine) through an approximate index such as HNSW. Keyword search scores chunks with BM25. A fusion step joins the two ranked lists; Reciprocal Rank Fusion uses only ranks, so the two score scales do not need to match. The result is the top-k candidate chunks.
steps.fixes: Hybrid retrieval finds both exact-term matches and paraphrases, so fewer relevant chunks are missed.
steps.out: Top-k candidate chunks with scores

evidence.ours: The human's diagrams show vector search; the keyword arm and the fusion step are ours (from the retrieval-algorithm catalogue and the Intelligent Educator plan).

steps.title: Rerank and refine: keep the few chunks that answer the question
steps.problem: First-stage retrieval is fast but rough. The top-k list has near-duplicates and off-topic chunks, and the LLM reads the start and end of a long context better than the middle.
steps.body: A reranker reads the question and each candidate together and scores them again; a cross-encoder or ColBERT late interaction is more exact than the first search. MMR removes near-duplicates. Refinement (CRAG) grades the chunks: if they are not relevant, the system retrieves again or from a new source, for example the web.
steps.fixes: The context that reaches the LLM is short, relevant and diverse, with the best chunks first.
steps.out: Top-n reranked chunks (n < k), or a 're-retrieve' signal

evidence.ours: The note about the middle of the context comes from the metric catalogue (Lost in the Middle), not from the human's diagrams.

steps.title: Generation: answer from the context, with citations
steps.problem: Even with good chunks, the LLM can ignore them, add facts that are not there, or answer in the wrong tone or language.
steps.body: The augment step puts the chunks into the prompt with their ids. The prompt asks the LLM to answer only from them, cite the chunk for each claim, and say 'I do not know' when the context is not enough. The prompt also sets voice, style and language. Active retrieval (Self-RAG, RRR) lets the model judge its own answer and ask for more retrieval when it is weak.
steps.fixes: Answers are grounded in the retrieved text, cite their source, and use the right voice.
steps.out: Answer with citations (or an abstention)

evidence.ours: 'Cite each claim' and 'abstain when the context is not enough' are our prompt rules.

steps.title: Caching layers: do not pay twice for the same work
steps.problem: Many users ask the same or nearly the same question. Each one pays for embedding, search and a long LLM call, and waits for all of it.
steps.body: Caches sit at several points. A query cache and a semantic cache return a stored answer when a new question is close enough in embedding space to an old one. An embedding cache and a vector-search cache skip repeated work in the middle. On the model side, prompt (KV) caching reuses the computed prefix of a long, fixed prompt, so only the new part is processed.
steps.fixes: Lower latency and cost for repeated questions, without a new LLM call when a safe match exists.
steps.out: A cached answer, cached vectors or search results, or a reused KV prefix

evidence.ours: Prompt / KV caching is ours; the human's diagram shows query, embedding, vector-search and LLM-response caches.

steps.title: Tracing and monitoring: see every step of every request
steps.problem: When an answer is wrong or slow, you cannot tell which step failed: the translation, the search, the reranker or the LLM.
steps.body: Each request gets a trace: one span per step, with input, output, latency and tokens. A tracing tool (Jaeger in the human's diagram; MLflow Tracing in our plan) stores the spans. Logs, metrics and a dashboard show response time, throughput (queries per second), error rate, chunking efficiency, embedding performance and retrieval quality over time.
steps.fixes: Failures can be found and attributed to one step, and slow or costly stages are visible.
steps.in: Spans and events from every step
steps.out: Traces, logs, metric time series, dashboards and alerts

evidence.ours: MLflow as the tracing tool is ours (Intelligent Educator plan); the human's diagram names Jaeger.

steps.title: Evaluation hooks: measure quality, not only speed
steps.problem: Monitoring shows that the system runs, not that it answers well. A change to the chunker or the prompt can make answers worse while every dashboard stays green.
steps.body: Evaluation hooks read the same traces. Offline, a fixed question bank runs after each change and scores retrieval (recall, nDCG) and answers (faithfulness, correctness, citations). Online, a sample of real traces goes to an LLM judge or a human. A judge must be checked against human labels before its scores are trusted.
steps.fixes: Each change is accepted or rejected on measured quality, and regressions are seen before users see them.
steps.in: Traces + a question bank with gold answers
steps.out: Scores per step and per question type; a pass/fail per change

evidence.ours: The human's diagram has 'retrieval quality' as a monitored metric; the offline/online evaluation hooks are ours.

graphrag.label: GraphRAG
graphrag.lede: The same stack, with a knowledge graph next to the text index: entities and relations are extracted at index time, and retrieval returns a subgraph (triplets) as well as passages. Based on the human's diagrams LLM-RAG-GraphRAG and GraphRAG-Formula (G-Indexing -> G-Retrieval -> G-Generation).

steps.title: G-Indexing: build a graph from the documents
steps.problem: Plain chunks lose the links between ideas. A question that needs facts from two chapters ('how does A depend on B?') finds each chunk alone, and never the connection.
steps.body: As in plain RAG, we chunk and embed. Then an LLM extracts entities and relations (and, in Microsoft GraphRAG, optional claims) from each chunk, and duplicates are merged into one node with one summarised description. The result is a knowledge graph 𝒢 whose nodes point back to their source passages. Microsoft GraphRAG also groups nodes into hierarchical Leiden communities and writes a report for each; LightRAG and HippoRAG skip communities.
steps.fixes: Relations between concepts become explicit, searchable edges, each linked to the text it came from.
steps.out: Knowledge graph 𝒢 (nodes, typed edges, provenance), community summaries, plus the text index

steps.title: The user asks a question
steps.problem: Same as plain RAG: restricted questions and restricted documents. A graph adds a new leak: one node can merge facts from documents with different access rights.
steps.body: The query service checks restrictions and notes the user's scope, as in plain RAG. For a graph, the scope must also apply to nodes, edges and community summaries, because a summary can mix text from several scopes.
steps.fixes: The question enters the graph pipeline with a scope that also filters the graph.
steps.out: An allowed question q with a user scope

evidence.ours: The graph-specific leaks come from the Intelligent Educator plan (access control), not from the generic diagrams.

steps.title: Query translation: find the entities in the question
steps.problem: A graph is searched from its nodes. The question text is not a node: we must find which entities it is about.
steps.body: It depends on the system. LightRAG asks the LLM for two levels of keywords: low-level (specific names) and high-level (themes). HippoRAG extracts the named entities of the question. Microsoft GraphRAG's local and global search use the question as it is; DRIFT expands it HyDE-style. Decomposition is useful again: a multi-hop question becomes a chain of smaller questions, each about one relation.
steps.fixes: The question now has anchor entities that the graph search can start from.
steps.out: Entities and keywords (low and high level), optional sub-questions

evidence.ours: Decomposition for multi-hop graph questions is ours.

steps.title: Routing: local, global or structured search
steps.problem: Some questions are about one entity ('what is X?'), some are about the whole corpus ('what are the main themes?'). One graph search does not answer both.
steps.body: A router picks the search mode. Microsoft GraphRAG has four: local search starts from the entities that match the question and collects their relationships, claims, community reports and text chunks; global search reads the community reports in a map-reduce pass; DRIFT starts global and follows up locally; basic search is plain top-k chunks. A question that maps to an exact pattern can become a graph query (text-to-Cypher, Neo4j).
steps.fixes: Entity questions get a focused subgraph; corpus-wide questions get summaries.
steps.out: A search mode (local, global, Cypher) and its parameters

steps.title: G-Retrieval: a subgraph plus passages, p_θ(G | q, 𝒢)
steps.problem: Text search alone returns separate chunks. It cannot follow 'A uses B, B is part of C' across documents.
steps.body: Entity linking maps the question's entities to graph nodes. From these seeds, a bounded walk collects the neighbourhood: k-hop expansion, Personalized PageRank (HippoRAG) or a prize-collecting Steiner tree (G-Retriever). The vector and keyword arms still run. The output is a small subgraph G of triplets, each with its source passages.
steps.fixes: Multi-hop evidence arrives together, as connected triplets with their passages.
steps.in: Entities, search mode, user scope; graph 𝒢 and text index
steps.out: Subgraph G (triplets) + passages + scores

steps.title: Prune and fuse: keep the paths that matter
steps.problem: A 2-hop walk from a popular node returns hundreds of edges. Most of them are noise, and they push the useful passages out of the context window.
steps.body: Path scoring ranks the paths from the seeds by relevance and length. Graph scores and vector scores are combined into one ranking. A cross-encoder or MMR then picks the final passages, as in plain RAG.
steps.fixes: The context holds a small, relevant subgraph and the passages that support it.
steps.out: Pruned triplets + top-n passages

evidence.ours: Peng et al. name knowledge enhancement (merging, pruning) and Microsoft local search ranks and cuts the context to a token budget; the path scoring and score fusion detail is ours (from the algorithm catalogue).

steps.title: G-Generation: answer from triplets and passages, p_φ(a | q, G)
steps.problem: Triplets alone are terse and lose nuance. Passages alone lose the structure. The LLM needs both, in a form it can read.
steps.body: The prompt lists the retrieved triplets as short lines and adds the passages they came from, with ids. The LLM answers and cites the passages, not the triplets, because a triplet is the extractor's reading of a passage. For global questions, community summaries are answered in parallel and then reduced into one answer.
steps.fixes: Answers follow the relations in the graph and still cite real text.
steps.out: Answer a with citations

evidence.ours: 'Cite passages, not triplets' is ours (it follows decision 2 of the Intelligent Educator plan: generated text is never evidence).

steps.title: Caching layers: the graph adds expensive work to reuse
steps.problem: Graph extraction and community summaries cost many LLM calls. Recomputing them, or the same subgraph for the same entities, wastes money.
steps.body: The same caches as plain RAG apply. In addition, extraction results are cached by chunk hash, and community summaries are computed once at index time. A cache shared across users is a leak risk if the cached answer used documents that another user may not read, so cache keys must include the scope.
steps.fixes: The graph is paid for once, and repeated questions are cheap, without cross-user leaks.
steps.in: Chunk hashes, question embedding, prompt prefix, user scope
steps.out: Cached extractions, summaries, answers and KV prefixes

evidence.ours: The cache layers are in RAG-Pipeline; 'caches shared across users' as a leak is from the Intelligent Educator plan; caching extraction by chunk hash is ours.

steps.title: Tracing and monitoring: add the graph spans
steps.problem: In GraphRAG there are more places to fail: the entity was not linked, the walk went too far, or the subgraph was empty.
steps.body: The trace gets spans for entity linking, traversal and pruning, with the seed nodes, the size of the subgraph and the time per step. Dashboards show the same service metrics as plain RAG, plus graph size and extraction cost.
steps.fixes: A wrong answer can be traced to a missing node, a bad link or a noisy walk.
steps.in: Spans from every step, including the graph steps
steps.out: Traces with seeds and subgraph size; dashboards

evidence.ours: The monitoring stack is in the human's production diagram; the graph spans are ours.

steps.title: Evaluation hooks: score the graph as well as the answer
steps.problem: A good answer can hide a bad graph, and a bad answer can come from a good graph. Answer scores alone cannot say which.
steps.body: Add graph checks to the plain-RAG hooks. Compare extracted triples with gold triples (precision, recall). Check whether the retrieved subgraph holds all the hops the question needs. For corpus-wide questions, use pairwise judge scores (comprehensiveness, diversity) and check the judge for position and length bias.
steps.fixes: We can tell whether GraphRAG helps because of the graph, and where it breaks.
steps.in: Traces, gold triples, a question bank with multi-hop items
steps.out: Graph scores, retrieval scores and answer scores per question type

evidence.ours: All of this step is ours (from the metric catalogue).

ie2.label: Intelligent Educator v2
ie2.lede: The thesis system, end to end, as the architecture plan of 2026-10-02 describes it. The plan's status is 'proposed': nothing below is built yet, except where a step says 'exists today'. Every component is from the plan; the order of the boxes and the plain-English wording are ours.

steps.title: Step 0: the evaluation harness comes first
steps.problem: If we build the system first and measure later, we cannot show that any part helps. Gold triples for the graph also take the longest to make.
steps.body: Both reviewers moved evaluation to the front. Step 0 builds a harness (run_eval --arm … --config …) that writes JSONL traces with a manifest hash, a typed question bank v0 of 50 items, a plain-LLM arm as the baseline, and a frozen corpus split. Gold-triple annotation starts now: sampled by relation and document, with negative links, two annotators and kappa.
steps.fixes: A baseline score exists on day 2, and every later arm is compared to it on the same questions.
steps.out: run_eval command, JSONL traces, manifest hash, plain-LLM baseline score

steps.title: Parse every document with Docling, and keep the figures
steps.problem: Today the partner platform parses PDFs (about 50 s per page), injects Chinese text, and discards figures. A textbook tutor must quote formulas and show figures.
steps.body: Docling parses every document, cached by file hash; PyMuPDF only renders and crops. Every figure, table and chart becomes an asset (crop, bbox, page, caption, neighbouring text); the caption and neighbouring text are indexed. Formula enrichment stays on, and the textbook batch runs on the IUST A100 slice. VLM picture descriptions are behind a flag: marked 'generated', never cited.
steps.fixes: Clean text in reading order, equations as LaTeX, and figures as citable assets.
steps.out: Parsed text, LaTeX formulas, asset records; parser acceptance-test numbers

steps.title: Chunk, embed on the university GPU, store locally
steps.problem: Embedding a textbook on an 8 GB Mac is slow, and the vectors must stay on the local machine.
steps.body: Chunks are written locally to chunks.jsonl with a content hash. On the IUST A100 slice, bge-m3 embeds them in batches into embeddings.parquet (model id, revision, hash). The file is loaded into the local Postgres with pgvector. Query time uses the same model and revision locally. Persian BM25 uses hazm normalisation. Only changed chunks are re-embedded.
steps.fixes: Dense and sparse vectors for the whole corpus, kept locally and reproducible from the manifest.
steps.out: embeddings.parquet → Postgres + pgvector; BM25 index (hazm)

steps.title: Typed extraction into a Postgres graph
steps.problem: Open relation extraction at textbook scale is the biggest unnamed risk (Fable's review), and a second graph database would be a second source of truth that drifts.
steps.body: Extraction runs against a closed concept vocabulary from the syllabus and slides, aligned to CSO / CS-KG. Nodes are Concept (with Method, Task, Metric, Dataset, Assumption), Example, Passage, Asset, Course, Lecture; relations include prerequisite-of, part-of, example-of, defines, uses. The graph lives in Postgres kg_nodes / kg_edges; experiments read hashed snapshots (networkx). Neo4j gets a one-way export for exploring only.
steps.fixes: One source of truth for the graph, a fixed vocabulary, and a snapshot hash in every run.
steps.out: kg_nodes / kg_edges, graph snapshot + hash, optional Neo4j export

steps.title: Access control: scope columns from the start
steps.problem: Different courses and cohorts must not see each other's material, and a graph can leak it through merged entities, mixed summaries and shared caches.
steps.body: Documents, passages, kg_nodes, kg_edges and assets get scope columns (course, cohort, visibility). Postgres row-level security, keyed to a membership table, also applies to pgvector search: filter before retrieval, never after. A citation guard lets an answer cite only passages the user can read. The thesis experiment has one course and one cohort, but the columns go in from step 0.
steps.fixes: No migration later, and a leakage test (canary strings, differential queries) in the harness.
steps.out: Scoped rows; filtered retrieval; citation guard

steps.title: The student asks in the tutor app
steps.problem: A student's follow-up ('and why is that?') makes no sense without the earlier turns.
steps.body: The existing FastAPI app and React shell (with Persian i18n) are kept. They already do query expansion and follow-up resolution, so the question that reaches retrieval stands on its own. Later, after the freeze, the tutor is launched from Moodle with LTI 1.3.
steps.fixes: A self-contained question, with the user's identity and scope.
steps.out: Resolved, expanded question

evidence.ours: The link to the multi-query explainer is ours: the plan says 'query expansion' without naming a method.

steps.title: Retrieval arms: compared on the same questions
steps.problem: The thesis must show whether a typed graph helps. That needs arms that differ only in retrieval.
steps.body: Arms: plain LLM (no retrieval); vector (pgvector + bge-m3 + BM25 with hazm + RRF + a local bge reranker); LightRAG as a baseline with corpus, chunks, embeddings, LLM and token budget frozen; typed-KG GraphRAG (entity linking → bounded typed traversal → passages → cited answer); hybrid (vector + typed-KG fusion). A question-type router comes only after the arms are frozen.
steps.fixes: A fair comparison: the same corpus, the same answer model, only the retrieval changes.
steps.out: Passages (+ subgraph where the arm has one) with scores

evidence.ours: Mapping 'bounded typed traversal' to the k-hop explainer is ours.

steps.title: Answer with one model for every arm
steps.problem: Different answer models per arm would confound the result: a better score could come from the model, not from the retrieval.
steps.body: A role → model table sets one model per role (parse_vlm, extract, classify, answer, judge), at temperature 0, with model ids pinned in each run manifest. The same answer model and the same judge serve every arm, and the judge differs from the answer model. The LLM calls go to AvalAI (OpenAI-compatible). Answers cite passages with page and asset thumbnail.
steps.fixes: Differences between arms come from retrieval, not from the model.
steps.out: Cited answer or abstention

steps.title: Caching: a deterministic cache key
steps.problem: Re-running an experiment must not cost the same LLM bill again, and a cache must not mix results of different models or prompts.
steps.body: The plan sets the cache key as model + prompt + input hash, with temperature 0, so an identical call returns the stored result. Extraction is estimated (tokens × price) before books are ingested. The plan names caches shared across users as a leak risk. It does not name a semantic cache or KV caching; those are not part of v2.
steps.fixes: Repeatable, cheap re-runs without mixing models or prompts.
steps.out: Cached LLM result or a new call

evidence.ours: The remark that semantic and KV caching are absent is our reading of the plan.

steps.title: Traces: the same records feed evaluation and the UI
steps.problem: If the demo, the thesis figures and the evaluation each keep their own logs, they will disagree.
steps.body: Every run writes JSONL traces: answer, citations, retrieved subgraph where the arm has one, latency and tokens, with a manifest hash. MLflow (already on the local hub) gives tracking and tracing for the harness; Metabase gives dashboards over eval results; Airflow can schedule ingest and re-index. Whether each service still starts is unverified.
steps.fixes: One trace record is the single truth for scores, figures and the demo.
steps.in: Spans and results of each run
steps.out: JSONL traces, MLflow runs, dashboards

steps.title: Evaluation: preregistered, stratified, human-checked
steps.problem: One RAGAS metric and one judge is too thin (Codex's review), and a judge can be biased.
steps.body: Measured: retrieval recall and nDCG, citation support (does the cited passage entail the claim?), answer correctness, abstention, latency and tokens. Stratified by question type, language, and whether the answer needs a figure, table, equation or multiple hops. Before running: the primary endpoint, hypotheses, power analysis and explicit criteria for 'GraphRAG is better'. Blinded human scoring on a sample reports judge-human agreement.
steps.fixes: A claim about GraphRAG that a reviewer can check and that was fixed before the data.
steps.out: Scores per arm and stratum; judge-human agreement

evidence.ours: Mapping 'citation support' to citation precision and the statistics tests to their explainers is ours.

steps.title: Compare page: a viewer of stored traces
steps.problem: A live side-by-side demo before evaluation is polish before proof, and two arms have no subgraph to show.
steps.body: The Compare page reads the stored run traces: answer, citations with page and asset thumbnail, the retrieved subgraph where an arm has one, latency and tokens, and the score when the question is from the bank. Thesis figures come from the same table. A 'run live' button comes later.
steps.fixes: The demo shows what was measured, not a new run that nobody scored.
steps.out: Side-by-side view per question

steps.title: After the freeze: Moodle launch and question export
steps.problem: Students use an LMS, but a full LMS integration adds no research value.
steps.body: After the freeze, and outside the thesis contribution: an LTI 1.3 launch only (pylti1p3) from Moodle in Docker, a Moodle question XML / GIFT export of the question bank, the VLM figure-description ablation, and a bank grown to 300-500 items. Canvas and Open edX are cut.
steps.fixes: The tutor can be linked from a course without changing the experiment.
steps.out: LTI launch link, GIFT export

arch._doc: Interactive architecture diagrams (2026-10-09, Brief G). components = what a box is (shared by all diagrams); diagrams = lanes of component ids + edges. 'only' = shown only in that mode (rag | graph); 'delta' = what changes in GraphRAG mode. Logos: ids of data/logos.json (Simple Icons) or null = neutral text badge. Sources: keys of stack.json sources or web_sources below. Built by build.py into stack-resolved.json (key 'arch').

user.name: User
user.what: The person who asks. In the human's diagrams the answer goes back to the same user, through the UI.
tradeoffs: What the user may see decides the access check later (row-level security), not the prompt.

ui.name: User interface
ui.what: The chat or search screen. It sends the question and shows the answer with its citations, and streams tokens so the wait feels shorter.
tradeoffs: Streaming hides latency but makes output checks harder: a check after generation needs the whole answer.
Showing citations builds trust only if they are correct; check citation precision.

mobile.name: Mobile service
mobile.what: A second client of the same query API. Named in the human's production diagram.
tradeoffs: Keep one API for all clients, so caching, tracing and access checks happen once.

admin.name: Admin service
admin.what: Where an admin uploads documents, starts re-indexing and manages users and their access labels.
tradeoffs: Re-indexing on every upload is simple but slow for large corpora; incremental indexing needs stable chunk ids.
admin.ours: The admin tasks (upload, re-index, access labels) are ours; the diagram names only the service.

query_svc.name: Query service
query_svc.what: The API that receives a question and runs the online pipeline: checks, cache, retrieval, prompt, LLM call.
tradeoffs: A thin service with an orchestration library is quick to build; a hand-written pipeline is easier to trace and test.

guard.name: Input guardrail
guard.what: Checks the question before any retrieval: is it in scope, is it allowed for this user, is it a prompt injection? If it hits a restriction, the system says so (in the HR example: 'go to HR') and stops.
tradeoffs: A rule list is cheap and predictable but misses paraphrases; a classifier model catches more but adds latency and false refusals.
Measure both sides: wrongly refused questions and wrongly answered ones.

qcache.name: Cache check
qcache.what: Before running the pipeline, look the question up: an exact match (same text) or a semantic match (an embedding close to an earlier question) returns the stored answer.
tradeoffs: A semantic cache saves the most but can return an answer to a different question when the threshold is loose.
Cache keys must include the user's access scope and the index version, or one user sees another's answer.

translate.name: Query translation
translate.what: Rewrites the question into a form the retriever handles better: several paraphrases (multi-query, RAG-Fusion), sub-questions (decomposition), a more general question (step-back) or a hypothetical answer to embed (HyDE).
tradeoffs: Each rewrite is one more LLM call: better recall, more latency and cost.
Rewrites can drift from what the user asked; keep the original question in the final prompt.
translate.graph: LightRAG extracts low-level (entity) and high-level (theme) keywords here; HippoRAG extracts the named entities of the query. Microsoft GraphRAG's local and global search do not rewrite the query; DRIFT expands it HyDE-style against community reports.

route.name: Routing
route.what: Chooses where the question goes: which data source (logical routing, an LLM picks the store) or which prompt (semantic routing, by embedding similarity).
tradeoffs: Wrong routes fail silently: the answer looks fine but comes from the wrong store. Log the route in the trace.
An LLM router is flexible but slow; an embedding router is fast but needs example questions per route.
route.graph: In GraphRAG the route picks the search method. Microsoft GraphRAG has four: local (about named things), global (about the whole corpus), DRIFT (both) and basic (plain top-k chunks). Neo4j adds Text2Cypher for exact structured questions.

construct.name: Query construction
construct.what: Turns the question into the query language of the chosen store: text-to-SQL for a relational database, text-to-Cypher for a graph database, or metadata filters for a vector store (self-query).
tradeoffs: Exact answers for structured questions (counts, dates, prerequisites) that similarity search gets wrong.
Generated queries can be invalid or unsafe: run them read-only, with a schema in the prompt and a row limit.

retrieve.name: Hybrid retrieval
retrieve.what: Finds the chunks most related to the question: nearest neighbours of the question embedding in the vector index, plus keyword matches (BM25), merged by rank fusion.
tradeoffs: Vectors find paraphrases but miss exact codes and names; BM25 finds exact terms but misses paraphrases. Hybrid fixes both at the cost of two indexes.
Approximate search (HNSW, IVF-PQ) trades a little recall for much lower latency.
Anthropic measured (2024-09-19): contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 cut top-20 retrieval failures by 49%, and 67% with a reranker.
retrieve.graph: GraphRAG links the question to entities first, then expands through the graph (neighbours, paths, communities); vectors still find the seed entities.
retrieve.ours: The keyword arm and fusion are not in the human's diagrams; they are from Anthropic's contextual retrieval post and the Azure guide.

rerank.name: Rerank + refine
rerank.what: Scores each retrieved chunk against the question with a stronger model and keeps the best few; refinement (CRAG) drops or corrects weak results and can trigger a new retrieval.
tradeoffs: A cross-encoder is much more accurate than the first-stage score but runs once per chunk: rerank tens, not thousands.
Fewer, better chunks shorten the prompt and reduce lost-in-the-middle errors.
rerank.graph: In GraphRAG this is knowledge enhancement: merge duplicate facts and prune the subgraph to the token budget (Microsoft local search ranks and filters entities, relations and reports to fit the context window).

augment.name: Augment
augment.what: Puts the selected chunks, their source ids and the instructions into the prompt (the 'context window' of the human's RAG-General diagram).
tradeoffs: More context raises recall but costs tokens and can bury the key passage.
Put stable parts (instructions, schema) first so the provider's prompt cache can reuse them.
augment.graph: GraphRAG puts graph data into the prompt: triplets, paths or subgraphs, formatted as tables, natural language or code-like text (Peng et al. list six formats).

generate.name: Generate
generate.what: The LLM writes the answer from the prompt and cites the chunk ids it used. With active retrieval (Self-RAG), it can ask for more evidence before answering.
tradeoffs: A larger model is more faithful but slower and dearer; route easy questions to a small model.
Self-hosting (vLLM, Ollama) keeps data local; an API is simpler to run.
generate.graph: G-Generation: the same LLM call, with graph context; Microsoft's global search first writes one partial answer per community report (map) and then merges them (reduce).

post.name: Output check
post.what: Checks the answer before it leaves: every claim has a citation, no restricted content, and the voice, style and language are right (the HR example does voice and style with fine-tuning).
tradeoffs: A second LLM pass catches more but doubles the cost of the answer; cheap rule checks (citation ids exist) first.
post.ours: The citation check is ours; the human's diagram has the restriction check and the voice / style / language step.

cache.name: Caching
cache.what: The human's pipeline names four caches: query cache, embedding cache, vector search cache and LLM response cache. Providers also cache the prompt prefix (KV cache) between calls.
tradeoffs: Every cache needs an invalidation rule: re-indexing must clear vector search and response caches.

docs.name: Private documents
docs.what: The source corpus (the human's 'private policy documents'; for the thesis, course material). Kept as raw files in object storage so the index can always be rebuilt.
tradeoffs: Keep raw files and the parsed text both: parsers improve, and re-parsing needs the originals.

parse.name: Parse + clean
parse.what: Turns files into clean text with structure: headings, tables, page numbers, figures. Bad parsing is the most common silent failure of RAG.
tradeoffs: Layout-aware parsers (Docling) keep tables and reading order but are slow; plain text extraction is fast but scrambles columns.
parse.ours: Parsing is not drawn in the human's diagrams; it is from the Azure and Google guides and the IE v2 plan (Docling).

chunk.name: Chunking
chunk.what: Splits the text into retrieval units: by characters, by sections, or by meaning (semantic splitter); hierarchical variants keep parent chunks or summary trees (RAPTOR).
tradeoffs: Small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding.
Contextual retrieval prepends a short LLM-written context to each chunk: better recall, one LLM call per chunk at index time.

embed.name: Embedding
embed.what: An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector. The question is embedded with the same model at query time (the human's note: 'this needs to be embedded itself too').
tradeoffs: Changing the model means re-embedding everything: version the index by model name.
Multilingual models (bge-m3) handle Persian and English in one space; domain fine-tuning helps narrow corpora.

vectordb.name: Vector index
vectordb.what: Stores the vectors with their chunk text and metadata, and answers nearest-neighbour queries fast (HNSW or IVF-PQ).
tradeoffs: A vector column in Postgres (pgvector) keeps one database and access control in SQL; a dedicated engine scales further and filters faster.
Index parameters trade recall, memory and build time.
vectordb.graph: GraphRAG also embeds entity descriptions and community reports here, so the graph can be entered by similarity (Microsoft GraphRAG uses LanceDB by default).

kwindex.name: Keyword index
kwindex.what: An inverted index of the same chunks for exact-term search (names, codes, numbers).
tradeoffs: Cheap and exact; needs a language analyser (stemming, Persian normalisation) to work well.
kwindex.ours: Not in the human's diagrams; from the Anthropic and Azure sources.

relational.name: Relational DB
relational.what: Users, access labels, document metadata, chat history and feedback. Also a target of text-to-SQL.
tradeoffs: Row-level security here can enforce who may see which chunk, if the vectors live in the same database.

kvstore.name: Cache store
kvstore.what: The fast key-value store behind the caches (Redis in the human's data layer).
tradeoffs: In-memory is fast but bounded: set a time-to-live and an eviction policy.

extract.name: Extract graph
extract.what: An LLM reads each chunk and writes the entities (name, type, description) and the relations between them; Microsoft GraphRAG can also extract claims (covariates). HippoRAG uses OpenIE triples; neo4j-graphrag can follow a given schema.
tradeoffs: The most expensive step of GraphRAG: one or more LLM calls per chunk (Microsoft adds 'gleanings' rounds).
A closed schema (fixed entity and relation types) gives a cleaner graph; open extraction finds more but is noisier.

resolve.name: Merge entities
resolve.what: Merges mentions of the same thing ('KG', 'knowledge graph') into one node and summarises its descriptions into one. HippoRAG adds synonymy edges instead of merging.
tradeoffs: Too little merging splits facts across nodes; too much merges different things. Measure entity-resolution F1 on a sample.

graphdb.name: Graph store
graphdb.what: Holds entities and relations (with links back to their source chunks) and answers traversals. Microsoft GraphRAG writes Parquet tables instead of a graph database.
tradeoffs: A graph database gives Cypher and fast traversals; Parquet tables plus an in-memory graph are simpler for batch use.
Keep chunk ids on every edge: answers must cite text, not just the graph.

community.name: Communities
community.what: Groups densely connected entities into communities, at several levels (Microsoft GraphRAG). LightRAG and HippoRAG skip this step.
tradeoffs: Communities make corpus-wide ('global') questions possible, but must be recomputed when the graph changes; LightRAG avoids this to allow cheap incremental updates.

reports.name: Community reports
reports.what: An LLM writes a report for every community (title, summary, key findings). These reports are what global search reads.
tradeoffs: One LLM call per community per level: a large part of the indexing cost.
Reports go stale when documents change.
LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft, 2024-11-25) skips these summaries at index time and moves the LLM work to query time.

gsrc.name: Graph source
gsrc.what: Where the graph comes from: an open knowledge graph (Wikidata, a curriculum ontology) or a graph built from the documents by the extraction steps.
tradeoffs: An open KG is clean but may not cover the course; a self-built graph covers it but has extraction errors.

gq.name: Query enhancement
gq.what: Gets graph handles from the question: named entities (HippoRAG), low- and high-level keywords (LightRAG), or sub-questions (decomposition).
tradeoffs: One LLM call; a missed entity here means the graph is entered at the wrong place.

link.name: Entity linking
link.what: Maps the question (or its keywords) to graph nodes, usually by vector similarity of entity descriptions.
tradeoffs: Fast and fuzzy; homonyms link to the wrong node. Keep the top few seeds, not one.

expand.name: Graph expansion
expand.what: Walks from the seed nodes: neighbours and relations (Microsoft local search, LightRAG one-hop) or Personalized PageRank over the whole graph (HippoRAG); collects the linked chunks too.
tradeoffs: More hops find multi-hop answers but the neighbourhood grows fast; PPR ranks the whole graph in one pass.

commsel.name: Pick reports
commsel.what: Global search: takes all community reports of one level, shuffled into batches that fit the context window. DRIFT: takes the top-K reports most similar to the HyDE-expanded question.
tradeoffs: A higher level means fewer, broader reports: cheaper, less detail.

mapreduce.name: Map-reduce
mapreduce.what: Map: each batch of reports gives intermediate points with a helpfulness score from 0 to 100 (0 is dropped). Reduce: the points are sorted by score, fill the context window, and the LLM writes one answer.
tradeoffs: Answers corpus-wide questions that top-k chunks cannot; costs many LLM calls per question.

drift_n.name: DRIFT loop
drift_n.what: A primer answer from the top community reports proposes follow-up questions; each follow-up runs a local search; results are ranked into the final answer.
tradeoffs: Better breadth than local search, cheaper than full global search; more steps to trace and debug.

gres.name: Retrieval result
gres.what: What graph retrieval returns: nodes, triplets, paths, subgraphs, or a hybrid with text chunks (Peng et al.).
tradeoffs: Triplets are compact but lose nuance; returning the source chunks next to them keeps the answer citable.

gfmt.name: Graph format
gfmt.what: Turns the graph result into prompt text. Peng et al. list five graph languages (adjacency / edge table, natural language, code-like forms, syntax tree, node sequence) and, separately, graph embeddings. Microsoft local search uses CSV-like tables of entities, relationships and reports.
tradeoffs: Tables are compact and easy to cite; natural language reads better for small models.

ggen.name: G-Generation
ggen.what: The LLM answers from the graph context. Peng et al. group improvements into pre-generation (better prompts), mid-generation (constrained decoding) and post-generation (checks and merges).
tradeoffs: The same faithfulness risks as plain RAG, plus errors baked into the graph at extraction time.

dashboard.name: Dashboard
dashboard.what: Panels for response time, throughput, error rate, cost and cache hit rate, with alerts.
tradeoffs: Averages hide slow tails: plot p95 and p99 latency.

metrics_n.name: Metrics
metrics_n.what: Counters and histograms from every service: requests per second, latency per stage, errors, tokens, cost.
tradeoffs: Cheap to keep for months; no per-request detail (that is what traces are for).

tracing.name: Tracing
tracing.what: One trace per question with a span for each stage (cache, retrieval, rerank, LLM call), so a slow or wrong answer can be traced to its stage.
tradeoffs: The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions are still in development; pin the version you use.

logging.name: Logging
logging.what: Structured logs of requests and errors, searchable (the ELK stack in the human's diagram).
tradeoffs: Do not log personal data or full prompts by default; mask them.

llmobs.name: LLM trace viewer
llmobs.what: Shows each trace with its prompt, retrieved chunks, answer, cost and evaluation scores; failing traces become new test cases.
tradeoffs: Self-hosted keeps prompts private; a hosted service is less work.
llmobs.ours: Not in the human's diagrams (which name Jaeger); MLflow is from the IE v2 plan.

feedback.name: User feedback
feedback.what: Thumbs up or down and corrections from users, stored with the trace id.
tradeoffs: Sparse and biased (unhappy users click more), but the only signal from real questions.
feedback.ours: Feedback capture is ours; the Google architecture has a quality-evaluation subsystem.

goldset.name: Test set
goldset.what: Questions with the expected answer and the chunks (or triples) that support it; grows from failing traces.
tradeoffs: Synthetic questions are cheap but easier than real ones; label a real sample by hand.
goldset.ours: The loop from traces to test cases is ours.

runeval.name: Run the pipeline
runeval.what: Runs every test question through the same pipeline as production and saves the traces.
tradeoffs: Fix the model version, prompts and index version, or results are not comparable.

retmetrics.name: Retrieval metrics
retmetrics.what: Did the right chunks come back, and near the top?
tradeoffs: Needs gold chunk ids; without them use an LLM judge for context relevance, and check the judge.
retmetrics.graph: Add graph metrics: triple recall of the evidence, all-hop recall for multi-hop questions, subgraph precision.

genmetrics.name: Answer metrics
genmetrics.what: Is the answer supported by the retrieved context (faithfulness), relevant, correct, and correctly cited? Often scored by an LLM judge.
tradeoffs: LLM judges have position and length biases; measure their agreement with human labels first.
genmetrics.graph: Microsoft GraphRAG compares answers pairwise on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment and directness.

kgq.name: Graph quality
kgq.what: Checks the graph itself: precision and recall of extracted triples, entity-resolution F1, schema conformance.
tradeoffs: Needs a hand-labelled sample of chunks; errors here cap every answer later.
kgq.ours: The surveys name the problem; this check list is ours, from the metric catalogue.

gate.name: Compare + release
gate.what: Compares the new version with the current one on the test set (with confidence intervals) and blocks a release that is worse.
tradeoffs: Small test sets give wide intervals: use paired tests on the same questions.
gate.ours: A release gate is ours; the IE v2 plan preregisters the comparison.

k8s.name: Container orchestration
k8s.what: Runs every service as a container and scales them (the outer frame of the human's production diagram).
tradeoffs: Kubernetes is heavy for one machine; Docker Compose is enough for a thesis prototype.

diagrams.title: Production architecture: layers and tools
diagrams.lede: The human's 'RAG in production' diagram, redrawn: the same layers, with the GraphRAG parts added and real tools on every box. Click a box for what it is, its trade-offs, tools and explainers.

diagrams.title: Ingestion and indexing (offline)
diagrams.lede: Top row of the human's RAG-Pipeline diagram (documents, chunking, embedding, vector database), with parsing and a keyword index added. In GraphRAG mode the graph-building row appears: extraction, entity merging, communities and their reports, all embedded back into the vector index.

diagrams.title: Retrieval and generation (per question)
diagrams.lede: Bottom row of the human's RAG-Pipeline diagram and the parts of RAG-Parts: guard, cache, query translation, routing, query construction, retrieval, rerank, prompt, LLM and an output check. Dashed arrows are the short cuts (refusal, cache hit) and the active-retrieval loop.

diagrams.title: Evaluation and observability
diagrams.lede: The brown boxes of the human's RAG-Pipeline (response time, throughput, error rate, retrieval quality) and the monitoring stack of the production diagram, joined to an offline evaluation loop: failing traces become test cases, and a release must not be worse than the current version.

diagrams.title: GraphRAG architecture
diagrams.lede: The frame of the Graph RAG survey (Peng et al. 2024; the human's Detailed-Introduction-GraphRAG figure): G-Indexing, G-Retrieval, retrieval result and format, G-Generation. Pick a method to see the path it takes; vectors stay in the loop as the way into the graph.

methods.name: Local search
methods.text: For questions about named things. The query is matched to entity descriptions in the vector store (LanceDB by default); the context mixes those entities, their relationships, claims (covariates), their community reports and the text chunks linked to them, ranked and cut to the token budget, as tables.

methods.name: Global search
methods.text: For questions about the whole corpus ('what are the main themes?'). Map: every batch of community reports at the chosen level gives rated points. Reduce: the top-rated points are merged into the answer.

methods.name: DRIFT search
methods.text: Global and local together: a primer reads the top-K community reports for the (HyDE-expanded) question and writes follow-up questions; each runs a local search; the results are ranked into the answer.

methods.name: Dual-level (hybrid)
methods.text: Keywords at two levels: low-level keywords find entities, high-level keywords find relations (both by vector match); one-hop neighbours are added. No communities, so new documents are merged into the graph without rebuilding it.

methods.name: Personalized PageRank
methods.text: Named entities of the query are linked to graph nodes; Personalized PageRank spreads from those seeds over the whole graph; passages are ranked by the probability of the nodes they contain. Single-step multi-hop retrieval.

checks.was: Plain RAG was one straight chain of ten boxes; caching, tracing and evaluation sat after 'Generate' as if they were steps 8 to 10.
checks.now: Caches, monitoring and evaluation are cross-cutting: they get their own layer (architecture) and their own loop (evaluation and observability).

checks.was: No query construction and no routing to several stores: every question went to the vector index.
checks.now: Routing chooses the store and query construction writes SQL, Cypher or metadata filters, as in RAG From Scratch and the human's RAG-Parts.

checks.was: No feedback loops: refinement (CRAG) and active retrieval (Self-RAG) were named but drawn as a straight line.
checks.now: Dashed loops from rerank back to query translation and from generation back to retrieval; refusal and cache-hit short cuts back to the user.

checks.was: One box 'Cache: semantic · KV' for all caching.
checks.now: The four caches of the human's RAG-Pipeline (query, embedding, vector search, LLM response) plus provider prompt caching, on a Redis cache store in the data layer.
The human's monitoring stack (Grafana dashboard, Prometheus metrics, Jaeger tracing, ELK logging) plus an LLM trace viewer (MLflow, Langfuse or Phoenix).

checks.was: Indexing was one box 'chunk · embed · store'; no parsing step and no keyword index.
